1380.title: Walking pilgrimage
1380.hook: the Camino to Santiago, Lourdes, Jerusalem: walking as prayer
1380.howItsDone: Christian pilgrims walk routes like the Camino to Santiago, often carrying a stamped pilgrim's credential, and visit places like Lourdes and Jerusalem to pray, attend Mass or services, and walk the stations of the cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Divine Office: prayer by the clock, day and night. Your line was the hours.

Tied to the back of a dusty backpack, a scallop shell bounces with every step. The person wearing it has blisters, a walking stick, and a little booklet that gets stamped in towns along the way. Ahead are more days of the same: up early, walk, eat, sleep in a bunk room full of strangers, walk again. The road is the Camino, the Way of Saint James, and it ends at a cathedral in Santiago, in the northwest corner of Spain. Ask walkers why they're doing it, and the answers run all over the place. Grief. Faith. A birthday. A divorce. No idea yet.
screen: `A SCALLOP SHELL ON A BACKPACK.` → `A BOOKLET STAMPED ALONG THE WAY.` → `GRIEF, FAITH, NO IDEA YET.`

segments.voice: A pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place, made as an act of devotion. Christians walk to many such places; here are three, and the thread that runs through them. First, Santiago. Tradition says the apostle James is buried there, and pilgrims walk to his tomb, some wearing the scallop shell as their sign. Second, Lourdes, in the south of France. Catholic tradition holds that Mary appeared there to a young girl named Bernadette, beside a grotto with a spring. Pilgrims come to pray, to bathe in the water, and to bring the sick. Third, Jerusalem. Christian pilgrims walk the Via Dolorosa, the way of sorrows, stopping to pray at stations along the route Jesus is remembered to have carried his cross. And the thread runs back into the Bible. Its Book of Psalms has a group of songs headed "A Song of degrees," which some readers take as songs for going up to Jerusalem. One of them begins: "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD." And then: "Our feet shall stand within thy gates, O Jerusalem." Our feet. Not our thoughts. On a pilgrimage the body does the praying: the distance, the weather, the ache in the legs, the strangers who share bread. Some walkers say the arrival matters less than they expected, and the road matters more. Prayer doesn't have to sit still. Here it gets up and walks.
screen: `SANTIAGO: THE SCALLOP SHELL.` · `LOURDES: THE GROTTO AND THE SPRING.` · `JERUSALEM: THE WAY OF SORROWS.` · `OUR FEET SHALL STAND.` · then, large: `I WAS GLAD WHEN THEY SAID UNTO ME.`

segments.voice: Choose a destination close by, a window, a doorway, a plant, a tree outside, and before you set off, name one thing you're carrying: a hope, a worry, a person. Walk to it slowly, the way you'd walk the last stretch to a cathedral, feeling each foot land. When you arrive, stay there; if you pray, offer what you carried, and if not, just let yourself arrive.
Walking pilgrimage. A journey on foot to a holy place, Santiago, Lourdes, Jerusalem, where the walking itself becomes the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: walking as prayer. Our feet shall stand within thy gates. See you tomorrow.

1381.title: Alone in the field
1381.hook: Rebbe Nachman of Breslov taught speaking to God in your own words, alone in nature
1381.howItsDone: Breslov Hasidim and others who practice hitbodedut set aside time each day, often outdoors or alone in a room, to speak to God aloud in their everyday language, alongside the fixed Jewish prayer services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, walking pilgrimage, and the psalm's line, our feet shall stand within thy gates. Your line was walking as prayer.

"And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." One quiet sentence in Genesis, right before Isaac looks up and sees the camels bringing Rebekah. What was he doing out there, alone, at dusk? The Bible doesn't say. Jewish tradition has an answer: he was praying. Much later, a Hasidic teacher, Rebbe Nachman of Breslov, made that picture a daily practice for anyone. Go out alone, he taught, into a field if you can, and talk to God, not in the words of a prayer book, but in your own. After these Christian ways of prayer, the path turns to Jewish ones.
screen: `ISAAC IN THE FIELD AT DUSK.` → `TRADITION: HE WAS PRAYING.` → `GO OUT ALONE, AND TALK.`

segments.voice: Rebbe Nachman's word for it is hitbodedut, which means making yourself alone: seclusion, time set apart. First, it's daily, and it's private. In his teachings, collected by his student Nathan, Nachman urges setting aside time every day to be alone, in a room or, better, out in the fields, and pour out your heart. He placed this practice very high among the ways of serving God. Second, your own language. Jewish prayer has its fixed services, in Hebrew, said at set times, and Nachman kept those. But in hitbodedut, he says, speak the language you actually speak, so the words come straight from the heart and you understand every one. Tell God everything, the way you'd talk to a close friend: what went wrong today, what you want, what you're ashamed of, what you're afraid of. Third, when the words don't come. Some days, his teaching says, you'll sit there and nothing will come out. Then say even one word, over and over. Even showing up and wanting to speak counts. Fourth, why a field. Nachman taught that when a person prays out among the grasses and plants, they join in the prayer and lend it strength. The field isn't scenery. It's company. And Isaac? The rabbis of the Talmud read his walk in the field as prayer, and connect him with the afternoon prayer, mincha, said as the day turns toward evening.

segments.voice: Step outside, open a window, or just face one, and talk out loud, quietly, in your own everyday words. If you pray, speak to God as you'd talk to a close friend; if you don't, speak to the open air, or to someone you love, or simply say what's true for you today. If nothing comes, say one word, and say it again.

1382.title: Kavanah, intention
1382.hook: Jewish prayer asks for kavanah, the heart aimed at what the lips are saying
1382.howItsDone: Jews who pray the set daily prayers try to bring kavanah, directed intention, to the fixed words; teachers in the tradition also speak of bringing it to blessings, meals and other daily acts.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hitbodedut: Rebbe Nachman's way of speaking to God in your own words, out loud, somewhere quiet. Your line was my own words.

Before they prayed, the pious ones of old would wait an hour. That's how the Mishnah, the collection of early Jewish law, describes them. Not to get the words ready. They knew the words. They waited to get the heart ready, to direct it toward their Father in heaven. Then the same passage turns strict. Once you've begun, even if a king greets you, don't answer him. Even if a snake is wound around your heel, don't stop. That's a great deal of attention for a few minutes of words.
screen: `THEY WAITED AN HOUR.` → `TO GET THE HEART READY.` → `NOT EVEN FOR A KING.`

segments.voice: The name for what they waited for is kavanah, usually translated intention, or directed intention: the heart aimed, the way you aim your steps down a road. The Mishnah uses this language of aiming; in one rule about reciting the Shema, the question is simply whether a person directed his heart. The roots reach into the Torah. Deuteronomy, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, asks Israel "to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul." The rabbis of the Talmud asked a sharp question about that line: what kind of service happens in the heart? Their answer was prayer. So prayer is the service of the heart, and kavanah is what makes it the heart's. Then a tension Jewish teachers have turned over for a long time. Jewish prayer has fixed words, said at fixed times. The fixed part has its own name, keva. Kavanah is the living part. Lean only on keva and the words run on autopilot. Wait only for kavanah and you might never get around to praying. The Mishnah names the danger in one line: whoever makes their prayer a fixed task, their prayer is not a plea. Yet the tradition doesn't throw out the fixed words because the heart wanders. It keeps the words, and keeps asking for the aim. And the idea reaches past prayer: Jewish teachers speak of kavanah in eating, in giving, in the small commanded acts of an ordinary day.
screen: `KAVANAH: THE HEART, AIMED.` · `PRAYER, THE SERVICE OF THE HEART.` · `FIXED WORDS, LIVING AIM.` · `NOT ONLY IN PRAYER.` · then, large: `TO SERVE HIM WITH ALL YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Pick one small act you can do right now: a sip of water, folding your hands, standing up from your chair. Before you do it, wait one breath, the way the pious ones waited, and know what you're about to do and why; if you pray, point it toward God, and if you don't, toward the person or the day it serves. Then do it slowly, all the way through, and nothing else.
Kavanah. Directed intention: the heart aimed at what the lips or hands are doing, in Jewish prayer and beyond it. Today's word.
Your line: kavanah. The same act can be done with the heart pointed at it, or on the way to something else. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1383.title: Character work
1383.hook: the Musar movement works on one character trait at a time
1383.howItsDone: People who practice Musar often choose one middah, a trait such as patience or humility, and attend to it for a period of time, with daily notes, study of Musar texts and short repeated phrases, sometimes in a small group.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was kavanah: the heart aimed at what the hands or lips are doing. Your line was kavanah.

Ask a friend who they'd like to become, and the list comes fast. More patient. More generous. Honest even when it costs something. Calmer in traffic. Kinder to their brother. Ask when they're starting, and the list goes quiet. Where would anyone begin with all that? A Jewish movement of teachers gave an answer so plain it can sound like a trick. Don't start with the list. Start with one line on it, and stay there a while.
screen: `A LIST OF WHO YOU'D LIKE TO BE.` → `WHERE WOULD ANYONE BEGIN?` → `ONE LINE ON THE LIST.`

segments.voice: The movement is called Musar. In the book of Proverbs, musar is a Hebrew word for instruction or correction. The King James gives the line: "My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother." Jewish teachers used the word for writing about character, and a rabbi named Israel Salanter made it the name of a movement. Its starting point: the traits of a person, in Hebrew middot, can be worked on like a skill. Not admired from far off. Practiced. Patience, order, humility, generosity, honesty, calm. A saying often attributed to Salanter puts the difficulty bluntly: it is easier to learn the whole Talmud than to change a single trait. So you don't try to change them all. You pick one, and watch it through the day, where it holds and where it slips. Some practitioners write a line about it each night. Some repeat a short phrase, often a line from a text, until it settles in. After a stretch, they move to the next trait. The movement stood on older Jewish wisdom. The Mishnah's Ethics of the Fathers asks who is mighty, and answers with Proverbs: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." Musar treats that inner work as the hard part, and the small daily gain as the real one.
screen: `MUSAR: INSTRUCTION, CORRECTION.` · `TRAITS CAN BE PRACTICED.` · `ONE TRAIT AT A TIME.` · `RULING YOUR OWN SPIRIT.` · then, large: `HE THAT RULETH HIS SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Let a short list pass slowly through your mind: patience, honesty, generosity, order, humility, calm. Don't choose the one you think you ought to; choose the one where yesterday went wrong, where you snapped, rushed, held back or covered something over, and name it in one plain word. If you pray, you can ask for help with it; if you don't, simply hold the word and let it sit with you.
Musar. Instruction, correction: a Jewish movement of character work, practicing one trait at a time. Today's word.
Your line: one trait. Not a new self by Friday, but a little more patience by the end of the month. See you tomorrow.

1384.title: Counting the Omer
1384.hook: Jews count seven weeks of days from Passover to Shavuot, some giving each day a quality
1384.howItsDone: Jews who keep the count say a blessing each evening from the second night of Passover and then state the day's number of the Omer until Shavuot; some also reflect on a kabbalistic quality assigned to that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Musar: character work, one trait at a time. Your line was one trait.

During Passover, in Jewish homes and synagogues, someone says a blessing in the evening and then one short sentence: today is one day of the Omer. The next evening: today is two days of the Omer. Then three. Then four. A number said out loud, and nothing else to do. No meal attached to it, no special clothes. Just the number, growing, all the way to the festival of Shavuot. And yet it has its own blessing, its own rules, and an old question about what happens if you forget.
screen: `TODAY IS ONE DAY OF THE OMER.` → `NIGHT AFTER NIGHT, A NUMBER.` → `ALL THE WAY TO SHAVUOT.`

segments.voice: The count comes straight from the Torah. Leviticus says, in the King James wording: "And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the sabbath, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven sabbaths shall be complete." That sheaf is the omer, an offering of new grain from the harvest. Seven weeks of days, counted one by one, then a festival: Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks. Passover remembers leaving Egypt. Shavuot, tradition says, remembers the giving of the Torah at Sinai. So the count walks a road, from being set free to being given something to live by. And it's a count up, not a countdown. A countdown treats the days in between as a waiting room. A count up adds each day to the total, so every one of them is kept. Over time a second layer grew. Some Jews, following the kabbalists, give each of the seven weeks a quality, starting with chesed, loving-kindness, and each day within the week a shade of those qualities: loving-kindness within loving-kindness, strength within loving-kindness. Then the rabbis add a very human question: what about someone who forgets to count for a whole day? One well-known ruling says keep counting, but without the blessing. A missed night doesn't send anyone back to the start.
screen: `THE SHEAF, AND SEVEN WEEKS.` · `FROM FREEDOM TO SINAI.` · `A COUNT UP, NOT A COUNTDOWN.` · `A QUALITY FOR EACH DAY.` · then, large: `SEVEN SABBATHS SHALL BE COMPLETE.`

segments.voice: Take the quality the count begins with, loving-kindness, and look for it in your last day: where it came easily, and where it stalled or went missing, without grading yourself. Then say quietly inside, the way a counter would: today is one. If you pray, you can hold that day before God; if you don't, just hold it in your attention, breath by breath.
Counting the Omer. Seven weeks of days, counted aloud one by one from Passover to Shavuot, and for some, a quality for every day. Today's word.
Your line: count the days. The count is too important to drop over one missed night. Until tomorrow.

1385.title: Blessings all day
1385.hook: a rabbi of the Talmud taught a hundred blessings a day, scattered through the ordinary hours
1385.howItsDone: Observant Jews say short blessings throughout the day, on waking, before and after eating, after using the bathroom, and on seeing or hearing things like thunder, the sea or good news, aiming for a hundred a day.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was counting the Omer: seven weeks of days, counted aloud one by one. Your line was count the days.

A hundred. That's the number Rabbi Meir named. A person, he taught, as the Talmud records, is obliged to say a hundred blessings every day. Not a hundred long prayers in a service. A hundred short sentences, scattered through the ordinary hours: on waking, before bread, after washing the hands, on hearing thunder. A hundred sounds like a great deal, until you see how small each one is, and how many things in an ordinary day could be stopped for and noticed.
screen: `A HUNDRED, SAID RABBI MEIR.` → `SHORT, AND SCATTERED.` → `WAKING, BREAD, THUNDER.`

segments.voice: You met the Jewish blessing back on day two hundred fifty; today, a whole day of them. A beracha has a shape people come to recognize. It opens by speaking to God directly, blessed are you, Lord our God, king of the universe, then names what's in front of the person: the one who brings bread from the earth, the one who creates the fruit of the vine. The Mishnah gives a whole chapter to blessings for things a person might meet: lightning and thunder, mountains and the sea, good news, and bad news too. The Talmud records a blessing for after using the bathroom, thanking God for a body made with openings that work as they should. Nothing is too ordinary to be noticed. A blessing comes before or alongside the thing, so it works like a small door. You don't just eat the apple. You stop, see that there is an apple, name where it came from, and then eat. The Talmud makes a striking claim: whoever enjoys something of this world without a blessing is like someone who has taken what belongs to heaven. The verse it leans on is from the Psalms, in the King James: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof." Read this way, a hundred blessings is less a quota than a way of walking through a day with the doors open.
screen: `THE SHAPE OF A BLESSING.` · `THUNDER, MOUNTAINS, BAD NEWS.` · `A SMALL DOOR BEFORE THE THING.` · `ENJOYING WITHOUT A BLESSING.` · then, large: `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.`

segments.voice: Look around slowly for five things: the chair under you, the air coming in, a sound from outside, your own hands, the light in the room, and stay with each long enough to really see it. If you pray, you can use the old opening, blessed are you, and name the thing; if you don't, simply say a quiet thank you for it inside. Five small stops.

1386.title: Study in pairs
1386.hook: Jewish learning is often done in pairs, arguing over a text
1386.howItsDone: In yeshivas and study halls, and in adult-learning programs, Jews study Talmud and other texts in pairs called chavrutas, reading aloud and questioning each other line by line.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was blessings all day: short blessings scattered through the ordinary hours. Your line was a hundred blessings.

Two men in the Talmud studied together: Rabbi Yochanan, a great teacher, and Resh Lakish, who, the story says, had once been a bandit before he turned to learning. Then Resh Lakish died, and Rabbi Yochanan was deeply pained. The rabbis tried to help. They sent him a sharp scholar to sit in the empty seat. Every time Rabbi Yochanan said something, the new partner answered: there's a teaching that supports you. Every single time. It should have been a comfort. It wasn't.
screen: `RABBI YOCHANAN AND RESH LAKISH.` → `AN EMPTY SEAT.` → `A PARTNER WHO ALWAYS AGREED.`

segments.voice: Here's what Rabbi Yochanan said, in the Talmud's telling. When I said something, Resh Lakish would raise twenty-four objections, and I would give twenty-four answers, and so the matter became clear. You tell me there's a teaching that supports me. Don't I already know I'm right? That's chavruta. The word is Aramaic, close to chaver, a friend or companion, and it means study in a pair. In a traditional study hall, pairs sit across a table, one text open between them, reading aloud and arguing. Not fighting: arguing toward the text. What does this line mean, why this word, what about the case it doesn't mention? The noise of a room full of pairs is part of the picture. The Talmud reaches for a verse from Proverbs, in the King James: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend." The rabbis read it of two students who sharpen each other in learning. And the Mishnah's Ethics of the Fathers gives advice in two short pieces: make yourself a teacher, and get yourself a companion. A partner who only nods leaves you where you started. A partner who pushes back makes you say why. This week turned from walking as prayer to Jewish ways: your own words, alone in a field; kavanah; Musar; the Omer; a hundred blessings. Today, the one practice that needs a second person across the table.
screen: `TWENTY-FOUR OBJECTIONS.` · `CHAVRUTA: A PAIR, ONE TEXT.` · `A TEACHER AND A COMPANION.` · `A WEEK OF JEWISH WAYS.` · then, large: `IRON SHARPENETH IRON.`

segments.voice: Take the line iron sharpeneth iron, say it once slowly, and ask what it means; then take the other side: when does a friend dull you instead of sharpening you? Let the two voices take turns and answer back, without hurrying. If you pray, you can bring the question before God; if you don't, just let the argument breathe.
Chavruta. Study in a pair: two people, one text, and plenty of questions across the table. Today's word.
Your line: two heads. The point of a partner isn't agreement. A week of Jewish ways, done.
